extracted.intended_audience: laypersons and home caregivers (non-physician) seeking practical guidance on recognition, prevention, and home nursing of common infectious diseases; also useful to nurses and general practitioners as a practical manual
extracted.subtask_description: Practical textbook guidance for recognizing, differentiating, preventing, and providing home nursing/supportive treatment for common infectious diseases (measles, German measles, smallpox, chickenpox, typhoid). Emphasizes incubation, characteristic signs, isolation, hygiene, symptomatic remedies, and prevention measures like vaccination and sanitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measles — home nursing and symptomatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive home/nursing measures to relieve fever, cough, and other symptoms and to prevent complications from measles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponge children with tepid water and adults with water at about 80 deg F every two hours as directed. Use hot packs when cough is incessant or rash is not well developed: strip patient and wrap from feet to neck in a blanket wrung out of hot water containing two teaspoonfuls of mustard per gallon, cover with two dry blankets for two to three hours, keep a cold cloth on the head. Cough mixture: syrup of ipecac 20 drops plus paregoric 1 teaspoonful for an adult (one-third dose for a six-year-old) in one-quarter glass of water, repeat every two hours. For hoarseness, rub neck with sweet oil (two parts) and oil of turpentine (one part) and cover with a flannel bandage. Instil boric acid solution (10 grains per ounce of water) into both eyes every two hours. Severe diarrhea: bismuth subnitrate one-quarter teaspoonful every three hours. Diet for adults: milk, broths, gruels, raw eggs; young children on milk mixtures should have mixture diluted one-half with barley water. Give nourishment every two hours except during sleep. Bed rest: patient should be ten days in bed; remain three days in room after getting up (or three weeks total if others at home may contract measles) and then stay in the house a further week after leaving the room. Emphasize avoidance of exposure to wet or cold drafts to prevent pneumonia or tuberculosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: German measles (rubella) — clinical features and differential signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristic incubation, symptom profile, rash progression, and distinguishing features versus measles and scarlet fever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incubation usually about two weeks (may vary 5–18 days). Rash often is first sign (especially in children); preliminary symptoms (if present) are milder and shorter than in measles: headache, sore/red throat, red spots on mouth, chilliness, muscle soreness, anorexia, watering eyes. Catarrhal symptoms are generally absent or mild; cough of measles is absent. Fever is often absent or mild (~100°F, rarely >102°F). Rash appears on face then chest and covers body in hours (within 24 hours), consisting of rose-red, round or oval slightly raised spots (pinhead to pea size) that may coalesce; eruption lasts about two days and may turn coppery as it fades. Enlarged glands (especially at back of neck) are common (~two-thirds of cases) and are a characteristic sign. Differentiation points from measles/scarlet fever include milder/shorter or absent prodrome, milder/absent fever, less catarrh and cough, more pronounced posterior cervical gland enlargement, milder sore throat than scarlet fever, and finer desquamation when peeling occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: German measles — management, isolation, and convalescent care
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended minimal treatment, isolation, diet, eye care, and household cleaning after German measles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Little or no treatment generally required. Keep patient in bed in a darkened room on a liquid diet while fever lasts and isolate indoors until eruption signs are passed. Treat eyes with boric acid as in measles. Diet: milk, broths, thin cereals, beef juice, raw eggs or eggnog for adults/older children; infants' milk mixtures diluted one-half with barley water. After disease passes: bath, fresh clothing for patient, thorough cleansing and airing of sick room and clothing usually sufficient; chemical disinfection generally unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallpox — contagiousness, epidemiology, and prevention emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Smallpox is extremely contagious; prevention by vaccination is paramount, and one attack or recent successful vaccination confers strong protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smallpox contagion is largely derived from scales and skin particles of patients and may be transmitted through the air from the sick room; direct contact not required. One attack almost invariably protects against another. Vaccination stands alone as the most effective preventive measure and should be performed early in life and repeated when epidemics threaten. Emphasize public-health measures (quarantine, vaccination campaigns) because individual vaccination is the principal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallpox — vaccination scheduling, revaccination, and post-exposure use
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended ages and timing for vaccination and guidance on revaccination and vaccination after exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every individual should be vaccinated between the second and third month after birth, again between ages ten and twelve, and at other times when an epidemic threatens. An unvaccinated person should be vaccinated and revaccinated until a successful 'take' occurs. Protection from a successful vaccination is variable but roughly lasts about four to five years; after ten to twelve years protection is generally lost. A person continuously exposed may be vaccinated every few weeks (harmless if repeated). An unvaccinated person exposed to smallpox can often escape the disease if successfully vaccinated within three days of exposure (but escape is not certain). A previously successfully vaccinated person may 'take' again any time after four or five years and should be revaccinated if exposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallpox — vaccination technique and criteria for successful vaccination
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical technique for vaccination in the absence of a physician and the expected local reaction timeline that defines a successful vaccination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform vaccination on outside of the arm a few inches below the shoulder. Wash arm thoroughly with soap and warm water, then alcohol diluted one-third with water; allow to evaporate without rubbing. Heat a cold needle point in a flame until red hot and use it (not touching it thereafter) to lightly scratch the skin (area about one-fourth inch square) removing only outer layer, not drawing blood; repeat at a second spot an inch or two below. Apply vaccine matter: squirt liquid vaccine on raw spots, or dip ivory points with dried vaccine in boiled-and-cooled water and rub over the raw places. Leave the arm bare and untouched until the raw spot is perfectly dry (~half hour). Cover with sterilized gauze for three days, thereafter protect with clean soft cotton/linen. If the scab is knocked off leave open sore and treat as wound. Expected course if vaccination 'takes': day 3—red pimple with surrounding redness; day 5—blister/pimple with depressed center and swelling; day 8—full rounded pimple containing 'matter' surrounded by large redness; from about day 11 the sore dries and a brown scab forms by ~day 14; scab drops at ~3 weeks leaving pitted scar. If the reaction is too slight or too rapid, repeat vaccination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallpox — detection and differentiation from other eruptions (notably chickenpox) and handling of mild cases
rubrics_metrics.description: How to recognize smallpox, common diagnostic pitfalls, and the public-health stance toward even mild cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smallpox can be mistaken for chickenpox or other skin eruptions in mild forms; the layman should rely more on the general symptoms and course (preliminary fever and system symptoms) than on rash appearance, which requires experience. Mild/modified cases are particularly dangerous to the community because they may be lightly judged; treat mild types as rigidly as severe cases with regard to isolation and quarantine. Historical notes: mild cases following vaccination ('varioloid') have much lower death rates but may still require caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallpox — nursing, isolation, and disinfection protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical nursing and household infection-control measures while caring for a smallpox patient and for handling contaminated items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarantine patient in an isolated building; remove unnecessary articles (carpets/furnishings) from the sick room; darken the room to lessen eye irritation. Diet: liquid (milk, broths, gruels). Analgesia/pain relief: laudanum 15 drops or paregoric 1 tablespoonful in water every three hours for adults in early days. Sponging: cool water as in scarlet fever; cold pack (sheet wrung out in water 68–75°F wrapped around naked body from feet to neck, tucked, covered with dry blanket, cold cloth or ice cap on head) may be used for an hour and repeated; cold sponging/pack indicated when temperature is over 102.5°F or when fever accompanied by restlessness/delirium. Maintain great cleanliness: change bedclothes daily, sponge patient 2–3 times daily with warm water unless fever high. Keep cloths wet with carbolic-acid solution (½ teaspoon per pint hot water) on face and hands; use face mask with holes and cover with oil silk to keep in moisture. Cut hair short; treat scalp crusts with carbolized vaseline. Instil boric acid into eyes and spray throat with Dobell's solution every few hours. Diarrhea in adults may be checked with teaspoonful doses of paregoric hourly in water. Do not reuse vaseline/cloths on another patient. All clothing, dishes, etc. contacting patient must be boiled, soaked in 2% carbolic-acid solution for 24 hours, or burned. Patient may reenter world only after all scabs have gone, bathing, and donning disinfected or new clothes outside the sick room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chickenpox — clinical features and distinguishing characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical incubation, eruption pattern, distinguishing features vs smallpox, course, and usual outlook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incubation commonly about two weeks (may vary 13–21 days). Eruption often the first sign; preliminary discomfort short or absent (in adults may be more pronounced). Fever usually 99–102°F. Lesions start on the body (especially back) as small red pimples that rapidly become pearly blisters (pea to fingernail size), often in successive crops (one distinguishing feature vs smallpox). Blisters rarely contain pus unless scratched; they dry in 3–4 days and form thin crusts which fall off leaving temporary red spots; pitting is rare. Eruption may occur on scalp, forehead, palms, soles, and in the mouth. Chickenpox usually results in rapid recovery in 8–12 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chickenpox — home management, prevention of scratching, and isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended supportive care for children with chickenpox and measures to prevent complications from scratching and spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep children in bed during eruptive stage until blisters have dried. To prevent scratching use calamine lotion, carbolized vaseline, or bathing with baking soda solution (1 teaspoonful to a pint of tepid water). Diet: as recommended for German measles. Isolate patient in the house until all signs of the eruption are passed; after recovery give a bath and fresh clothes before mingling. Thoroughly clean and air the sick room; chemical disinfection not essential. Physician services are desirable to ensure the case is not a mild smallpox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — causes, modes of transmission, and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal sources and routes by which typhoid is spread and practical preventive measures to avert epidemics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typhoid is caused by a germ attacking intestines and sometimes blood. Principal epidemic source: contamination of water supply through bad drainage. Preventive measures: boil drinking water whenever typhoid is prevalent; avoid uncooked food; control flies (they carry germs from discharges to food, vegetables, milk); ensure milk handlers and milk containers are clean; avoid raw oysters from polluted waters; recognize that dust, ice (freezing does not kill the germ), contaminated clothing, utensils, door handles, and other fomites can spread infection. Typhoid germs escape chiefly in bowel discharges and urine, sometimes in sweat, saliva, and vomitus. Proper disposal of excreta and good sanitation, protected water supply, and preventing flies and sewage contamination are imperative to prevent epidemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — clinical course, warning signs, complications, and convalescence guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical incubation, progression of fever and other signs, important danger signs, common complications, duration, and the critical importance of rest in bed early in illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incubation commonly 8–23 days. Typical onset gradual with increasing daily fever pattern (evening higher than morning) progressing over first week; average duration about one month. Early symptoms: lassitude, headache, backache, anorexia, sometimes chill in adults or convulsion in children, belly pain, occasional vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, coated/brownish cracked tongue. Pink-red 'rose spots' about pinhead size on chest and belly that disappear on pressure and may recur during weeks 2–3 are characteristic. Second-week delirium, wandering at night, dusky flushed face, brown-coated tongue, abdominal distention and tenderness, 'pea-soup' diarrheal stools with offensive odor are typical. Complications: pneumonia, perforation and bleeding of the intestines; bleeding occurs in 4–6% of cases and accounts for ~15% of deaths; perforation in 1–2% and causes ~10% of deaths. Relapse occurs in ~10% of cases. Danger signs: prolonged very high fever (105–106°F), marked delirium, tremors, bleeding from bowels, sudden intense abdominal pain with vomiting (possible perforation), rapid feeble pulse, stupor. Emphasize strict bed rest early — patients who walk about in the first week are much more likely to die.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever — detection: limits for lay diagnosis and role of laboratory testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how a nonphysician can assess probability of typhoid and the definitive diagnostic test timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A layman cannot be absolutely certain of typhoid in any given patient, but when symptoms follow the general course described a probability is established. Unusual types are difficult to diagnose clinically; a physician may rarely be certain before the end of the first week or ten days. Examination of the blood provides an exact method of determining the presence of typhoid and is useful around the end of the first week/ten days.
